title: "CAPA: root cause to effectiveness check"
order: 17

## The ticket

Wednesday. The Owen Pruitt deviation record is closed — discovery, containment, extent-of-condition,
disposition, and a documented "yes, reportable" call are all filed, exactly where `deviations-and-
nonconformances` left them. Your Quality Analyst drops a new document on your desk: the CAPA
(corrective and preventive action) investigation the deviation record's CAPA decision opened.

It's short. One paragraph:

> **Root cause:** Brookfield staff did not verify that the deferred-donor list in the downtime
> binder was current before using it during Friday night's downtime event.
> **Corrective action:** Retrain Brookfield collection staff on the downtime procedure.

She's ready to route it for sign-off. You've seen this exact shape of write-up before — on the IT
side, it's the ticket that closes "root cause: user error, action: additional training," and you
already know how that one ages. Ask the question an assessor would ask next: if you retrain
Brookfield's staff today, and the exact same Friday night happens again — same maintenance window,
same binder, same stale list — does anything go differently? On the facts as written, no. That's
the tell. This write-up hasn't found the root cause yet; it's found a place to stop looking.

"Push it one more level," you tell her. "What you've written is where the failure surfaced. I want
to know why it was there to surface."

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

This module lives in **QSE 9** of AABB's Quality System Essentials framework — **Process
Improvement** (an older AABB template titled it "Process Improvement Through Corrective and
Preventive Action," which is exactly the ground this module covers). CAPA stands for **corrective
and preventive action**: the process that turns "we know what happened" into "we've proven it can't
happen the same way again."

The failure mode this QSE exists to prevent is the one your draft write-up just walked into: an
organization that documents a *cause* without ever finding the *root* cause, closes the file, and
discovers eighteen months later that the exact same failure mode produced a second event — at a
different site, with a different donor, and a CAPA file that shows the org already "fixed" this
once. An assessor reading two CAPAs for the same underlying gap, a year apart, doesn't read that as
bad luck. They read it as a quality system that investigates events without ever touching the
system that produces them.

You already run half of this discipline under a different name. CAPA is **problem management** —
root cause analysis, the permanent-fix half of the incident/problem split you use every week. Module
2 was the other half: **incident management**, restore service, contain the immediate problem,
decide what happens to this specific unit. Problem management exists because incident management,
run well, still leaves the underlying cause untouched — service is restored, but the same root
cause produces the same incident again unless something separately fixes it. CAPA is that separate
motion, applied to a regulated process instead of a service.

Here's the piece ITIL practitioners routinely skip that this QSE makes mandatory: **proving the fix
worked.** A problem record in most shops closes when the permanent fix ships. CAPA doesn't get to
do that — it stays open until someone checks, later, with real data, whether the failure mode
actually stopped. That's the **effectiveness check**, and it's this module's headline skill.

One more bridge, worth naming because you'll hear the phrase constantly once you start reading
deviation and CAPA files: **"root cause: human error" is the quality world's "closed: user error"**
ticket resolution code. You already treat that resolution with suspicion in your own incident
reviews — not because people never make mistakes, but because "user error" so often means "we
stopped looking at the point where a human touched it, instead of asking why the system let that
touch cause harm." A CAPA log that leans on "human error" gets read by an inspector with exactly
that same suspicion, for exactly the same reason.

## The CAPA process in plain English

CAPA has four moving parts, in order: **root cause analysis**, then a **corrective action**, then a
**preventive action**, then an **effectiveness check**. Skip the order and the whole thing falls
apart — you can't pick a real corrective action until you know the real cause, and you can't check
effectiveness against a criterion you never wrote down.

**Root cause analysis.** The goal is to keep asking "why" past the first answer, until you land on
something that's actually *systemic* — a gap in a process, a control, or a system design — rather
than a description of a person's behavior in the moment. AABB's framework treats this as central to
Process Improvement; a common, well-known technique for doing it is the **5 Whys**: state the
problem, ask why it happened, take that answer and ask why *it* happened, and keep going — typically
five rounds, sometimes fewer, sometimes more — until further "why" questions stop producing new
system-level answers. (A **fishbone diagram**, also called an Ishikawa diagram, is the other
common tool — it sorts candidate causes into categories like people, process, equipment, and
materials, useful when a failure has several plausible contributing branches instead of one linear
chain. This event has one clean chain, so 5 Whys is the better fit; you'll want the fishbone
approach for messier events later.)

Run it on Brookfield:

1. **Why did Owen's donation get accepted at Brookfield despite an active deferral?** Because the
   printed deferred-donor list in Brookfield's downtime binder was four days stale — dated the
   previous Monday — and didn't include Owen's deferral, entered the following Tuesday.
2. **Why was the list four days stale?** Because the version of the downtime procedure in
   Brookfield's binder didn't require pulling and printing a fresh deferred-donor list immediately
   before a downtime event — it only called for a periodic refresh on a set calendar.
3. **Why was that outdated refresh requirement still what Brookfield was following?** Because
   Brookfield's binder held a **superseded revision** of the downtime SOP — an earlier version that
   predates whatever later revision, if any, tightened the refresh requirement.
4. **Why did a superseded revision survive in active use at a live collection site?** Because
   nothing in Lakeshore's document-control process confirms, and tracks, that every satellite
   site's physical binder copy was actually swapped for the current revision when the SOP was last
   updated. Distribution to remote sites runs on an honor system — someone is supposed to replace
   the page — not on a verified, acknowledged handoff.
5. **Why does document control have no verified distribution step for satellite-site procedure
   copies?** Because the document-control system has no mechanism — no review-date trigger, no
   required acknowledgment, no periodic reconciliation — tied specifically to *controlled paper
   copies used during downtime events at remote sites*, where there's no BECS connection to catch a
   stale version the way there might be at a networked site. **This is the root cause**: a
   document-control gap, not a Brookfield staffing or training gap. Staff followed the binder in
   front of them correctly, every step.

Compare that to your QA's first draft, which stopped after step 1. "Staff didn't check the list was
current" isn't wrong — it's just the *symptom*, restated as if it were the explanation. Push past it
and the actual finding is uncomfortable in a more useful way: this isn't a Brookfield problem. It's
a Lakeshore document-control problem that happens to have surfaced first at Brookfield.

**Corrective action** fixes the instance in front of you — the specific failure mode, at the
specific site where it was found. For Brookfield: replace the binder's downtime SOP with the current
revision immediately, and get the site lead's signed, dated acknowledgment that it's been swapped —
not "the binder was mailed," but confirmation it's physically in place and the old page is gone.
That's necessary. It's also not sufficient, because it does nothing about every other site that
might be running the identical superseded revision right now.

**Preventive action** is where the root cause actually gets addressed, because the root cause was
never "Brookfield's binder" — it was "no verified distribution process for satellite-site downtime
procedures." Two preventive actions follow directly from the root cause, and both trace straight
back to the extent-of-condition question module 2 raised and deliberately left open:

- **Extent-of-condition check, now:** audit every other Lakeshore satellite site's downtime binder
  for the same exposure — is the current SOP revision physically present, and is the deferred-donor
  list refresh cadence what the current procedure requires? Fix, on the spot, any site found holding
  a superseded copy.
- **The system fix:** a change to how Lakeshore's document-control process handles controlled paper
  copies at remote sites — for example, a document-control system enhancement that ties satellite
  binders to a tracked distribution list with required acknowledgment of receipt, or an automated
  review-date trigger that flags any site whose binder hasn't been confirmed current since the last
  SOP revision. That's a real change to a controlled process (and possibly a system), which means it
  doesn't get implemented informally — it becomes a change request and goes through formal change
  control, the subject of the next module. CAPA's job stops at *deciding* this fix is needed and
  handing it off with a clear description of what has to change and why; walking it through
  approval, implementation, and verification is `change-control-for-regulated-systems`'s job, not
  this one.

**Effectiveness check** is the part almost everyone shortcuts, and it's this course's headline
skill for a reason. An effectiveness check has four required pieces: a **measurable criterion**, a
**time window**, a **data source**, and a **pre-agreed definition of failure** — written down before
you check, not decided afterward depending on what you find. "Confirmed the binder was replaced" is
not an effectiveness check. It confirms *implementation* — that the action happened — which is a
different, easier question than whether the action *worked*.

A real effectiveness check for this CAPA: **at Lakeshore's next scheduled document-control audit of
all collection sites, roughly six months after the corrective and preventive actions are
implemented, zero sites are found holding a superseded revision of any downtime procedure or a
deferred-donor list older than the current SOP's required refresh point.** The data source is the
audit's site-by-site findings, owned by Quality. The pre-agreed failure definition is explicit: even
one out-of-compliance site at that audit means the CAPA is **not** effective — reopened or extended,
not quietly closed with a note about "one outlier."

Notice what makes that check genuinely capable of failing. It doesn't ask "was the fix rolled out" —
you already know that from the corrective/preventive action records. It asks a question about the
world *after* the fix that could come back either way, checked by someone independent of the people
who implemented it, on a schedule set in advance.

CAPA closure follows from that check, and it has three possible outcomes, not one: **close** it if
the effectiveness check passes clean; **extend** it — same actions, more time or a wider check — if
the data is inconclusive or the interval was too short to tell yet; or **reopen** it as a new,
escalated CAPA if the check fails outright, because a failed effectiveness check means the root
cause wasn't the real one, or the action didn't actually address it. An inspector who finds a CAPA
"closed" the same week its corrective action was implemented, with no effectiveness data anywhere in
the file, has found a CAPA that was never actually verified — only completed. And a backlog of CAPAs
sitting open past their effectiveness-check date, untouched, is its own finding: it tells an assessor
the organization opens CAPAs it doesn't have the discipline to close correctly.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(c), last sentence | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph c" | A thorough investigation — including conclusions and followup — of any unexplained discrepancy or failure to meet specifications, made and recorded. Already quoted in full in `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`. | The regulatory floor under root cause analysis itself: a discrepancy write-up that stops at "staff didn't check the list" hasn't produced the "conclusions" this clause demands. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(f) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-one, paragraph f" | States that biological product deviations, *whether or not reportable*, "should be investigated" per Parts 211, 606, and 820 — deliberately guidance-tier language ("should"), inside a regulation otherwise full of "must." | Worth reading closely for the word choice alone: even FDA's own reporting rule signals that investigation *depth* — root cause, CAPA structure — is expected practice, not a codified "shall." |

That's a short table on purpose. This module's investigation-depth requirement is the same
606.100(c) clause module 2 already introduced, applied differently — to *why*, not *what*. There's
no new citation carrying CAPA's structure, because Part 606 doesn't name one.

## The actual text

606.100(c)'s last sentence, already quoted in full earlier in this course, worth isolating here
because it's doing different work than it did in module 2. Quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.100.md`:

> A thorough investigation, including the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained discrepancy
> or the failure of a lot or unit to meet any of its specifications shall be made and recorded.

Module 2 read this as the requirement to investigate *at all*. Read it again for root cause: the
word is **conclusions**, plural, with **followup** named separately. A one-line cause statement
("staff didn't check the list") isn't a conclusion in the sense this clause means — it's an
observation. The conclusion is the systemic finding (the document-control gap); the followup is the
corrective and preventive actions and the effectiveness check that proves they worked.

606.171(f), quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.171.md`, worth reading for its word choice as much
as its content:

> This part supplements and does not supersede other provisions of the regulations in this chapter.
> All biological product deviations, whether or not they are required to be reported under this
> section, should be investigated in accordance with the applicable provisions of parts 211, 606,
> and 820 of this chapter.

**Should**, not **shall** — inside a regulation that uses "must" eleven times in the same section.
That's not sloppy drafting; it's the regulatory text itself marking investigation depth as expected
practice rather than a codified mandate. This is worth stating plainly, because it's a genuine
regulation-versus-standard distinction, not a technicality: **21 CFR Part 606 never uses the words
"corrective," "preventive," or "root cause."** CAPA — as a named, structured process with those four
specific stages — comes from AABB Standards' Process Improvement QSE, not from Part 606's text. The
regulatory hook underneath the whole CAPA structure is 606.100(c)'s "conclusions and followup" and
606.171(f)'s "should be investigated." Everything else — 5 Whys, corrective versus preventive,
effectiveness checks with a defined failure criterion — is AABB Standard and accepted industry
practice sitting on top of that floor, not FDA regulatory text spelling out a methodology. Keep the
tiers labeled when you talk to your CIO about this: the law says "investigate thoroughly and record
your conclusions"; AABB's Standards say "here's the structured process that satisfies that."

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

A CAPA file that would survive a real assessor's read has four things, and any one missing is a
finding — again, independent of whether the underlying event caused harm.

**Documented root cause analysis, not a one-line cause statement.** The assessor wants the actual
reasoning — the 5-Whys chain or its equivalent — not just the final answer. "Root cause: document-
control gap," with no visible path to that conclusion, reads the same as no analysis at all: you
can't tell whether it's real or guessed.

**Actions that map to the stated root cause, both types present.** If the root cause is systemic (a
gap that could exist elsewhere) and the action file shows only a Brookfield-specific fix, that gap
between diagnosis and response is visible on its own — the preventive half is simply missing.

**An effectiveness check that was actually performed, with a real pass/fail record** — not a CAPA
closed the same week the action was implemented, with "verified complete" standing in for "verified
effective." The assessor wants the check's date, the data pulled, and the explicit call: pass or
fail against the pre-agreed criterion.

**A CAPA log with aging visible.** An open CAPA past its effectiveness-check date, with no update,
is itself a finding — it says the organization doesn't track its own commitments, which undercuts
every other CAPA in the file, closed or not.

## Common traps

**"Root cause: human error. Corrective action: retrain staff."** This is the dead end your QA's
first draft walked into, and it's the single most common gap in real CAPA files. It fails a simple
test: if the same circumstances recurred exactly, with the retrained staff back on shift, would
anything go differently? For Brookfield, no — the binder would still hold the wrong revision, and
retrained staff would still follow it correctly, straight into the same gap. "Human error" is a
description of where the failure surfaced, not an explanation of why the system let it surface
there.

**Corrective action without preventive action.** Fixing Brookfield's binder and calling the CAPA
done addresses one instance of a failure mode that, by the root cause itself, is plausibly sitting
at every other satellite site. A CAPA that stops at the corrective step has fixed the symptom
someone happened to find, not the system that produced it — and the next site to surface the same
gap makes the first CAPA look, in hindsight, like it never understood its own cause.

**An effectiveness check that can't fail.** "Confirmed the new binder was distributed to all sites"
is implementation evidence, not an effectiveness check — of course the binders were distributed, or
the corrective action wasn't done. A check that can't fail isn't measuring anything. "Confirmed the
current procedure is actually in place and being followed correctly at all sites, verified at the
next scheduled audit" can fail, which is exactly what makes it worth checking.

## What this means for your job

- **Read past the first "why" on every CAPA your QA brings you.** If retraining, reminding, or
  re-emphasizing a procedure is the entire corrective action, ask what changed about the process
  itself — not the person.
- **Ask explicitly whether a CAPA's preventive action was scoped to "everywhere this root cause
  could exist," not just "where it was found."** A single-site fix for a systemic cause is a red
  flag on its own, independent of how good that single-site fix is.
- **Never sign off on a CAPA's effectiveness check before asking what data it's based on and
  whether it was written down before the check ran.** An effectiveness criterion decided after
  looking at the results isn't a check — it's a rationalization.
- **Track CAPA aging as its own metric, not a footnote.** An open CAPA sitting past its
  effectiveness-check date is a finding you should surface before an assessor does.
- **When a fix requires changing a controlled process or a system, expect it to leave CAPA and enter
  change control.** A CAPA that tries to implement its own fix informally, without a change record,
  is a gap you should catch before it becomes someone else's finding.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA proposes closing this CAPA with "corrective action: retrain Brookfield staff on checking the deferred-donor list before every donor." Is retraining a legitimate corrective action here?

No. Retraining addresses a person's behavior, and the root cause analysis showed the people
involved didn't do anything wrong — they followed the binder in front of them correctly. The actual
root cause is a document-control gap: no verified process ensures satellite-site procedure binders
hold the current revision. Retraining Brookfield's staff changes nothing about whether the next SOP
revision reaches every site's binder reliably. A corrective action has to change the process that
produced the failure, not add instructions for the people who were already following the process as
given to them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: True or false: 21 CFR Part 606 requires Lakeshore to run a formal CAPA process with documented root cause analysis.

False, as worded. Part 606's text never uses the words "corrective," "preventive," or "root cause" —
the regulatory hook is 606.100(c)'s requirement for a "thorough investigation... including
conclusions and followup," plus 606.171(f)'s "should be investigated" language, both of which set an
expectation without specifying a methodology. The structured CAPA process — root cause analysis,
corrective and preventive action, an effectiveness check — comes from AABB Standards' Process
Improvement QSE (binding on Lakeshore through accreditation) and from accepted quality-system
practice, not from Part 606's own words. Don't tell your CIO "the FDA requires a CAPA process" —
tell them FDA requires a documented, conclusive investigation, and AABB's Standards are what turn
that into the specific four-stage process this lesson just walked through.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Your QA wants to close this CAPA as soon as Brookfield's binder is replaced and the other sites' audit comes back clean. Reasonable?

No — that closes on implementation, not effectiveness. Confirming the actions happened is necessary
but answers a different question than whether they worked. This CAPA's effectiveness check is a
scheduled, independent re-check — at the next document-control audit, roughly six months out — that
looks for the same failure mode across every site, with a pre-agreed rule that even one site found
non-compliant means the CAPA isn't effective yet. Closing the day the actions are implemented skips
the one step that actually distinguishes a CAPA from a to-do list: proving, later, with real data,
that the fix held.
:::

## Where this goes next

Two of this CAPA's actions are still just decisions on paper: Brookfield's binder swap and the
other-sites audit can happen right away, but the real system fix — a document-control process or
system change that ties satellite-site procedure copies to a tracked, acknowledged distribution —
can't just be switched on. It has to go through **`change-control-for-regulated-systems`**, the next
module, which picks up exactly where this one stops: turning a CAPA's "here's what needs to change"
into a formally requested, assessed, approved, and verified change.
